overview: This file combines a brief 1941 narcotics report from the Bechuanaland Protectorate, transmitted through the League of Nations and the U.S. State Department in 1942, with a much larger body of 1930 material on opium policy in Japanese-ruled Taiwan (Formosa). The Taiwan documents present competing perspectives on the colonial opium-licensing and monopoly system: an American consular survey, public petitions, a physicians’ memorial favoring medical treatment over additional licenses, and an extensive Government-General defense of gradual suppression supported by statistics, administrative detail, and the text of ordinances and enforcement regulations. Together, the records document narcotics control as an international, diplomatic, medical, and colonial-governance issue.
interest: Shows conflicting Taiwan opium-licensing views, contrasted with routine Bechuanaland drug-control reporting.
